analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and lets investors adjust gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote; it died at the end of the 104th Congress in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top tax rate on long-term investment profits (capital gains) from 28 percent to 15 percent for individuals and from 34 percent to 15 percent for corporations. It would also let owners of stocks and business property raise the 'cost basis' of assets they have held for more than a year to account for inflation, shrinking the taxable gain when they sell. A lower 7.5 percent rate would apply to gains earned by low- and middle-income taxpayers, and the small capital-loss deduction would be inflation-adjusted.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations holding appreciated stocks and business property — that is, mainly investors with substantial assets. Gains taxes would drop by nearly half, and inflation adjustments would erase tax on the portion of a gain that merely kept pace with prices. Small savers whose gains fall within the 15-percent income bracket would pay a reduced 7.5 percent rate on that slice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors holding appreciated stocks and property

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the maximum individual capital gains rate from 28 percent to 15 percent, with a 7.5 percent rate on the first slice of gains for taxpayers in the 15-percent income bracket [S2][S3].
Reduces the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent [S2][S3].
Reduces the alternative minimum tax rate applied to capital gains to 15 percent [S3].
Indexes the basis of corporate stock and business capital assets held more than one year, so gains attributable to inflation are not taxed [S2][S3].
Indexes the $3,000 annual limit on deducting capital losses for noncorporate taxpayers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenues would fall, so other taxpayers would eventually bear more of the burden or the deficit would grow. Because capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households, most of the tax cut would flow to them.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is concentrated: capital gains income is held overwhelmingly by wealthier households, so the largest dollar benefits would go to them while the lost revenue would be borne by all taxpayers [S2].

Indexing only the basis and not taxing inflation-adjusted gains narrows the tax base permanently; the bill's transition rule also applies immediately to sales after December 31, 1994, adding revenue cost [S3].

Indexing applies to corporate stock and business property but excludes depreciation adjustments, and it does not cover ordinary savings assets like a creditor's interest, so the relief is uneven across asset types [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The modest benefits for low- and middle-income taxpayers (the 7.5 percent rate and the indexed loss limit) are real but small compared with the bill's main effect: a large, permanent tax cut on investment profits that mostly accrues to the wealthiest households, paid for through lost federal revenue. As drafted, the distribution of benefits skews heavily toward those who already hold appreciated assets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 104th Congress and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it simply expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, with no further action recorded [S5].
No vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury and taxpayers who do not hold large appreciated assets were better off, since the near-halving of the capital gains rate never took effect; investors lost the opportunity.

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 4, 1995 and never reported it out, so it never reached the House floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no partisan split appears in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Investors in corporate stock and business assets
industries.note: The bill nearly halves the tax on investment profits and erases tax on inflation-only gains. Because stock and business-asset gains are concentrated among wealthier households, the benefit would mostly flow upward while lost revenue is spread across all taxpayers [S2][S3].

The corporate capital gains rate would drop from 34 percent to 15 percent, and the corporate minimum tax on gains would fall accordingly, cutting taxes for companies selling appreciated property [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Regulated investment companies, REITs, and mutual fund investors
industries.note: Fund vehicles and REITs could pass through indexing adjustments to their shareholders in proportion to the indexed assets they hold, extending the inflation break to fund investors [S3].
